clips.text: Odin tells Frigg that he intends to visit Vafþrúðnir. The giant's wisdom is famous, and Odin wants to test it for himself.
clips.speaker: Narrator

clips.text: I would rather keep you here among the gods. I know no giant equal to Vafþrúðnir in strength of understanding. This journey may end badly.
clips.speaker: Frigg

clips.text: I have travelled widely and learned much. I would know how great his wisdom is.
clips.speaker: Odin

clips.text: Experience has not quieted Odin's desire to learn. It has brought him to the threshold of another contest.
clips.speaker: Narrator

clips.text: Go safely, then, and return safely. May your mind be sharp in the exchange of words ahead.
clips.speaker: Frigg

clips.text: Frigg sees that advice will not keep him back. Odin enters the giant's hall under the name Gagnráðr.
clips.speaker: Narrator

clips.text: Greetings, Vafþrúðnir. I have come to discover whether you are truly wise.
clips.speaker: Odin

clips.text: Who is this stranger speaking in my house? Unless you prove wiser than I am, you will not leave it alive.
clips.speaker: Vafþrúðnir

clips.text: The welcome has become a challenge.
clips.speaker: Narrator

clips.text: I am a thirsty traveller. I ask for hospitality after my journey.
clips.speaker: Odin

clips.text: Come forward, then, and take a place to sit.
clips.speaker: Vafþrúðnir

clips.text: A poor man entering a wealthy person's hall should say what is useful or keep silent. Too much talk before a hard-hearted listener can turn against its speaker.
clips.speaker: Odin

clips.text: The god does not announce his authority. He occupies the dangerous position of a guest who must establish his value through answers, with no assurance that courtesy will protect him.
clips.speaker: Narrator

clips.text: Tell me the name of the horse that brings day to humankind.
clips.speaker: Vafþrúðnir

clips.text: Skinfaxi. His shining mane illuminates the world.
clips.speaker: Odin

clips.text: And the horse that carries the night?
clips.speaker: Vafþrúðnir

clips.text: Hrímfaxi. Foam falls from his bit at morning and becomes dew in the valleys.
clips.speaker: Odin

clips.text: Day and night are not abstractions in this exchange. They move through the world with named animals, visible effects, and a place in a remembered order that both speakers must know.
clips.speaker: Narrator

clips.text: What river divides the gods' territory from the giants'?
clips.speaker: Vafþrúðnir

clips.text: Ífing. It runs open and never freezes.
clips.speaker: Odin

clips.text: What is the field where Surtr and the gods will meet?
clips.speaker: Vafþrúðnir

clips.text: Vígríðr. A hundred leagues it stretches in every direction. That is the field appointed for their battle.
clips.speaker: Odin

clips.text: The questions have moved from the daily passage of light to the place of the final battle. A correct answer requires knowledge of the catastrophe appointed within the world.
clips.speaker: Narrator

clips.text: You are learned, guest. Let us sit together and stake our heads on which of us is wiser.
clips.speaker: Vafþrúðnir

clips.text: Then tell me where earth and heaven came from.
clips.speaker: Odin

clips.text: The earth was made from Ymir's flesh, the mountains from his bones, heaven from his skull, and the sea from his blood.
clips.speaker: Vafþrúðnir

clips.text: Beneath the ordered world lies the body of a primordial being. The giant knows the ancestry of the landscape because it is bound to the ancestry of his own kind.
clips.speaker: Narrator

clips.text:
We shall wager our heads
here in the hall,
guest, on our wisdom.
clips.speaker: Vafþrúðnir

clips.text: Tell me the origins of sun and moon, of day and night, of winter and summer.
clips.speaker: Odin

clips.text: Mundilfari is the father of the heavenly lights. Dellingr belongs to the account of day, Nörvi to that of night. Vindsvalr is winter's father, and Svásuðr is summer's.
clips.speaker: Vafþrúðnir

clips.text: The exchange is patterned and formal. Odin numbers his questions, and the giant answers without hesitation. Each successful reply postpones the moment at which one of them must fail. The names unfold an ancestry for the changing seasons and the measures of time.
clips.speaker: Narrator

clips.text:
From Ymir’s flesh
the earth was fashioned,
and from his bones the mountains.
clips.speaker: Vafþrúðnir

clips.text: Who was oldest among the giants? How did Aurgelmir come into being, and how could he have descendants without a giant woman?
clips.speaker: Odin

clips.text: Venomous drops came from Élivágar and grew into the first great being. Beneath his arm a man and woman grew. One foot begot a six-headed son with the other.
clips.speaker: Vafþrúðnir

clips.text: This is a world before human measures of ordinary birth. Vafþrúðnir treats the strange genealogy as knowledge inherited and held, not a riddle to be explained away.
clips.speaker: Narrator

clips.text: What is the earliest event you remember?
clips.speaker: Odin

clips.text: I remember Bergelmir, born long before the earth was made. I remember his being placed upon a lúðr.
clips.speaker: Vafþrúðnir

clips.text: That last word is difficult: a wooden vessel, or perhaps a mill-like container. The ancient object is less clear than later storytellers sometimes make it. What matters here is the reach of the giant's memory. He speaks from a depth of time beyond ordinary listeners, making the stranger's challenge increasingly formidable.
clips.speaker: Narrator

clips.text: Whence comes the wind that passes unseen over the sea?
clips.speaker: Odin

clips.text: At the edge of heaven sits Hræsvelgr in the form of an eagle. The movement of his wings sends wind over the world.
clips.speaker: Vafþrúðnir

clips.text: And Njörðr? How did he come among the Æsir, when he was not born one of them?
clips.speaker: Odin

clips.text: He was made among the Vanir and given as a hostage to the gods. When the world reaches its end, he will return to his own people.
clips.speaker: Vafþrúðnir

clips.text: Even a question about present company carries a future departure inside it.
clips.speaker: Narrator

clips.text: Tell me of the warriors in Odin's hall.
clips.speaker: Odin

clips.text: They go out to fight each day. They strike one another down, then return restored to sit together.
clips.speaker: Vafþrúðnir

clips.text: How do you know the hidden arrangements of gods and giants so well?
clips.speaker: Odin

clips.text: I have travelled through the worlds, as far as Niflhel beneath the earth.
clips.speaker: Vafþrúðnir

clips.text: His learning is not merely a collection of stories received from others. His journeys match the travel with which Odin justified leaving home.
clips.speaker: Narrator

clips.text: Who will remain of humankind after the terrible winter?
clips.speaker: Odin

clips.text: Líf and Lífþrasir will shelter in Hoddmímir's wood. Morning dew will sustain them, and human generations will descend from them.
clips.speaker: Vafþrúðnir

clips.text: How can the sun return after the wolf has taken it?
clips.speaker: Odin

clips.text: Before her death she will bear a daughter. That daughter will follow her mother's path in the sky.
clips.speaker: Vafþrúðnir

clips.text: The old world will be broken, but these answers preserve continuities that destruction cannot wholly consume.
clips.speaker: Narrator

clips.text: Who will inhabit the gods' dwellings after Surtr's fire?
clips.speaker: Odin

clips.text: Víðarr and Váli will remain. Móði and Magni will possess Mjölnir after Thor has fallen.
clips.speaker: Vafþrúðnir

clips.text: And what will bring death to Odin at the world's ending?
clips.speaker: Odin

clips.text: The wolf will kill the father of men. Víðarr will avenge him by tearing apart the monster's jaws.
clips.speaker: Vafþrúðnir

clips.text: The names of sons answer the question of what survives the fathers. Still in disguise, Odin has listened to the sentence of his own death.
clips.speaker: Narrator

clips.text: Vafþrúðnir is still answering correctly. Odin does not bargain for another outcome. Instead, he brings the contest toward something no traveller could have discovered. The giant's journeys reach deep beneath the earth, and his memory reaches back beyond its making. But one question remains outside all that learning.
clips.speaker: Narrator

clips.text: What did Odin whisper into his son's ear before the body was placed on the funeral pyre?
clips.speaker: Odin

clips.text: At once the giant knows who has been questioning him. No one else can know that private utterance. The question names the edge of his immense learning, and reveals the visitor's identity.
clips.speaker: Narrator

clips.text: No one knows what you said in your son's ear. With a doomed mouth I have spoken ancient lore and the doom of the gods.
clips.speaker: Vafþrúðnir
Vafþrúðnir

clips.text: There the poem stops. The stakes make the consequence plain, but it describes no blow, no execution, and no journey home to Frigg. Nor does it disclose the whispered words. Odin wins by asking about knowledge that belongs to him alone, not by obtaining an answer that will overturn his fate.
clips.speaker: Narrator

clips.text: The giant's last recognition leaves both triumph and unease in the hall. One speaker has lost the contest. The other has heard how he will die, and still keeps the secret that made him victorious.
clips.speaker: Narrator
